'''''Muehlenbeckia astonii''''', commonly known as the '''shrubby tororaro''', is an [[Endemism|endemic]] New Zealand [[shrub]] in the family [[Polygonaceae]]. It is found in both the [[North Island|North]] and the [[South Island]]s and has distinctive small heart-shaped [[deciduous]] leaves amidst a tangle of wiry interlocking branches. Although common in cultivation around the world, it is extremely rare and threatened in the wild. Its conservation status is "Nationally Endangered".

== Description ==
Shrubby tororaro has very small leaves (only {{convert|2|–|15|mm}} wide) on a {{convert|3|–|10|mm}} brown stalk, growing in clusters of two to three (sometimes five), or alternating along the longer branchlets. The leaves are usually dented at the tip and heart-shaped.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=de Lange |first=Peter J. |date=2014 |title=Muehlenbeckia astonii |url=http://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora_details.aspx?ID=113 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230220121947/https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/muehlenbeckia-astonii/ |archive-date=20 February 2023 |access-date=13 April 2018 |website=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network}}</ref> They are bright green above and pale below.<ref name=":1" />

Unlike most New Zealand plants ''M. astonii'' is leafless in winter. It grows from a distinct trunk, and has many fine reddish brown to orange flexible branches that zigzag around one another to form a dense, interwoven ball, generally {{convert|2|-|3|m}} around, and sometimes 4 × 4 metres.<ref name=":0" /> Older plants have stems like canes growing from the interior.<ref name=":2" /> Plants have been recorded living for over 80 years.<ref name=":5" />

Its flowers, appearing December to January, are tiny and grow in clusters of two to four, less than {{convert|10|mm}} in diameter, and are greenish to white or pinkish white. The plant is [[Plant reproductive morphology|gynodioecious]]: individuals have either female flowers or what have been described as 'inconstant male' hermaphrodites.<ref name=":0" /> 'Inconstant males' can self-fertilise, but their seeds have less than 5% viability. Isolated female plants produce infertile fruits, or hybridise with other ''Muehlenbeckia'' species nearby.<ref name=":5" />

Fruits appear in October to June. The seed is a dark three-sided nut, about {{convert|2|-|2.5|mm}} long, dull not glossy (which distinguishes it from the scrub pōhuehue or torararo, ''[[Muehlenbeckia complexa|M. complexa]]'').<ref>{{Cite book|title=Small-leaved shrubs of New Zealand|last1=Wilson|first1=Hugh|last2=Galloway|first2=Tim|publisher=Manuka Press|year=1993|isbn=978-0-473-01851-1|location=Christchurch, New Zealand|pages=127–128}}</ref> The seed is surrounded by the remnants of the [[Tepal|tepals]], which swell into a white fruit in just 10–15 days.<ref name=":0" /> These fruits are sugary and edible, eaten by birds and lizards (which disperse the seeds), and by mice (which pulverise and kill the seed). Seeds can persist for up to four years in the soil.{{Sfn|Wotton|2018}} The plant is an important host for several endemic moth species, and in some cases their sole host.<ref name=":5" /><gallery mode="packed" widths="300" heights="250">

== Taxonomy ==
''Muehlenbeckia astonii'' was first described by botanist [[Donald Petrie (botanist)|Donald Petrie]] in 1911, and named ''Muehlenbecki Astoni'' after [[Bernard Aston]], who collected the specimens in [[Palliser Bay]] at the mouth of the [[Wainuiomata River]] in 1908.{{Sfn|Petrie|1911|pp=254–257}} The type specimen is in [[Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa]], Wellington. 

=== Etymology ===
The name "shrubby tororaro"<ref name=":5" /> distinguishes it from the similar species tororaro (''[[Muehlenbeckia complexa]]''), a scrambling plant with no trunk. It sometimes goes by the names '''wiggy-wig bush,'''<ref group="note">According to Given (2001), this name was coined by Marlborough farmer Ted Reynolds in 1996 referring to an igloo-like plant on his property.</ref> '''zig zag plant,'''<ref name=":4" /> '''wirebrush,'''<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.terrain.net.nz/friends-of-te-henui-group/trees-native-botanical-names-m-to-q/wirebrush-muehlenbeckia-astonii.html|title=T.E.R:R.A.I.N – Taranaki Educational Resource: Research, Analysis and Information Network – Muehlenbeckia astonii (Wirebrush)|website=www.terrain.net.nz|language=en|access-date=2018-05-06}}</ref> '''shrubby pōhuehue''',<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last1=de Lange|first1=Peter|last2=Jones|first2=Cathy|date=2000|title=Shrubby tororaro (''Muehlenbeckia astonii'' Petrie) recovery plan 2000–2010|url=http://www.doc.govt.nz/Documents/science-and-technical/tsrp31.pdf|journal=Threatened Species Recovery Plan|volume=31}}</ref> or '''mingimingi''' (a generic term for many small-leaved shrubs).<ref name=":5" />

== Distribution ==
This species was probably once widely distributed in the drier lowland and coastal parts of eastern New Zealand, especially on terraced riverbeds, possibly as far south as the Waitaki Valley, South Canterbury.<ref name=":0" /> Its former range is hard to determine, as the species was only recognised by botanists decades after most of New Zealand's dry scrublands had been cleared for agriculture.<ref name=":5" /> Its deep root system helps it survive in dry conditions, and can grow on open rocky hillsides and stony ground, up to {{convert|300|m}} altitude.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title=Know your New Zealand…Native Plants|last=Metcalf|first=Lawrie|publisher=New Holland|year=2009|isbn=978-1-86966-205-9|location=Auckland|pages=64–65}}</ref> It prefers free-draining, warm, sunny slopes, on moderately- to highly-fertile soil.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Given|first=David R.|date=2001|title=The Wiggy-wig bush – orphan or geriatric? ''Muehlenbeckia astonii'' (Polygonaceae) in North Canterbury and Marlborough|journal=Journal of the Canterbury Botanical Society|language=en|volume=35|pages=48–51|issn=0110-5892|hdl=10182/1254}}</ref> ''M. astonii'' is currently only found in four areas:<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" />

# Around [[Palliser Bay]] at the southern tip of the [[North Island]], from Honeycomb Light south to Sinclair Head. 
# Northeastern [[Marlborough Region|Marlborough]], currently only from the lower Awatere Valley, the Blind River, [[Clifford Bay]], and [[Cape Campbell]].
# Some sites in [[Canterbury, New Zealand|North Canterbury]] discovered in the 1950s and 1960s: Balmoral, [[Weka Pass]], Waikari Stream, [[Waiau, Canterbury|Waiau]], and along the [[Waipara River (Canterbury)|Waipara River]].
# [[Kaitorete Spit]] at [[Lake Ellesmere / Te Waihora|Lake Ellesmere]] (containing 90% of the world population), and [[Birdling's Flat]] and [[Lake Forsyth]] at the southwestern edge of [[Banks Peninsula]].

== Cultivation ==
<!--
[[File:Muehlenbeckia astonii kz1.jpg|thumb|300x300px|Pruned specimens of ''M. astonii'' at [[Auckland Botanic Gardens]]]]-->
''M. astonii'' is usually deciduous, though retains some leaves when grown in northern New Zealand. It prefers dry conditions, and is very drought-tolerant – excessive moisture can lead to root rot.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite book|title=100 Best Native Plants for New Zealand Gardens|last=Eadie|first=Fiona|publisher=Random House|year=2001|isbn=978-1-86962-150-6|location=Auckland|pages=166–168}}</ref> Its unusual form and wiry orange stems make it an interesting garden plant. It tolerates light shade, but grows well as a shelter plant in exposed situations, tolerating salt spray, wind, and frost. It can be planted as an informal hedge, and responds well to being pruned into shape.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://jury.co.nz/2015/09/22/plant-collector-the-curious-native-muehlenbeckia-astonii/|title=Plant collector: the curious native ''Muehlenbeckia astonii''|last=Jury|first=Mark and Abbie|date=22 September 2015|website=Tikorangi the Jury Garden|access-date=13 April 2018}}</ref> If planted in rich soil, ''M. astonii'' can grow vigorously upwards and may require staking. It can be propagated by winter hardwood cuttings, which strike best in early spring, and grows well from outcrossed seed.<ref name=":5" /> The translucent fruits are considered decorative, so most plants sold in nurseries are female.<ref name=":3" />

At a time when only 48 ''M. astonii'' were known to be growing wild in the Wellington area, the city councils of the [[Hutt Valley]] and [[Wellington]] began propagating plants from the wild and successfully growing males and females close together in traffic islands, each representing a different wild population, where they could pollinate each other. Traffic island populations were used as a stock to propagate 1500 plants from cuttings, and these were subsequently planted in [[Turakirae Head|Turakirae Reserve]] where the species once occurred.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Greening the city: bringing biodiversity back into the urban environment.|last=Sawyer|first=John|publisher=Royal New Zealand Institute of Horticulture|year=2005|editor-last=Dawson|editor-first=M. I.|location=Lincoln, Canterbury|pages=111–117|chapter=Saving threatened native plant species in cities — from traffic islands to real islands}}</ref>

== Conservation ==
''M. astonii'' is now rare in the wild. In most of the sites it is known from there are only 1–3 old plants, and almost no seedlings: male and female flowers occur on separate plants and need to cross-pollinate, so isolated individuals cannot reproduce.<ref name=":0" /> Several small populations show no out-crossing because males and females are too far apart.<ref name=":5" /> Most of the population (2,500 of 2,800) occur on private land at [[Kaitorete Spit]] south of [[Lake Ellesmere / Te Waihora|Lake Ellesmere]], and even at Kaitorete there are very few young plants.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=http://www.endangeredspecies.org.nz/store/doc/Muehlenbeckia%20astonii%20Endangered%20species%20factsheet.pdf|title=Shrubby Toroaro|author=Endangered Species Foundation|website=Endangered Species Foundation}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite web|url=http://www.doc.govt.nz/nature/native-plants/shrubby-tororaro/|title=Shrubby tororaro|website=Department of Conservation Te Papa Atawhai|access-date=16 April 2018}}</ref> Most wild populations are unlikely to recover without active management.<ref name=":5" /> 

Originally ''M. astonii'' would have grown in the dry scrub habitat known as "grey scrub", in association with grasses or sedges and small-leaved shrubs such as ''[[Bush lawyer (plant)|Rubus squarrosus]]'' (leafless lawyer), ''[[Olearia solandri]]'' (coastal tree daisy), and ''Discaria toumatou'' ([[Discaria toumatou|matagouri]]).<ref name=":0" /> These habitats were some of the first in New Zealand to be cleared for agriculture during colonisation, and so most individual ''M. astonii'' now are surviving in heavily modified open grassland.<ref name=":2" /> Plants suffer from trampling and browsing by livestock and other introduced mammals such as [[European rabbit|rabbits]], [[European hare|hares]], and [[Common brushtail possum in New Zealand|possums]], and seedlings are eaten by slugs and snails.<ref name=":0" /> Some plants have been seen succumbing to scale insects and fungal disease.<ref name=":5" /> Plants also have to compete with introduced grasses which smother them as seedlings, and with introduced shrubs such as boxthorn (''[[Lycium ferocissimum]]'').<ref name=":4" />

Open agricultural land is a poor habitat for shrubby tororaro, but is suitable for the other scrambling and climbing members of the genus (''M. complexa'' and ''M. australis'') which both compete with and hybridise with ''M. astonii''.<ref name=":5" />

This species was not recognised as endangered in the wild until the 1980s, and a recovery plan was created in 2000.<ref name=":2" /><ref name="DOC">{{cite web | url = http://www.doc.govt.nz/upload/documents/science-and-technical/tsrp31.pdf| title = Shrubby tororaro (''Muehlenbeckia astonii'' Petrie) recovery plan 2000–2010| author = P. de Lange| author2 = C. Jones| year = 2000| publisher = Department of Conservation, Wellington, New Zealand }}</ref> Its conservation status in 2004 was "Nationally Vulnerable", revised in 2009 to "Nationally Endangered".<ref name=":0" /> Representatives from all remnant populations of ''M. astonii'' have been propagated in large numbers, for both restoration planting on protected land, including [[Mana Island (New Zealand)|Mana Island]], and for gardens and urban planting projects.<ref name=":5" /> Three wild populations (at Cape Campbell, Balmoral Conservation Area, and Kaitorete Scientific Reserve) have legal protection and are undergoing restoration.<ref name=":6" /> Once threats are removed, wild populations of ''M. astonii'' appear to respond rapidly, so there is an excellent chance that this endangered species will recover.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Norton|first=David|date=2001|title=Re-establishment of the shrubby tororaro (''Muehlenbeckia astonii'' Petrie), a nationally threatened plant|url=http://nationalparks.co.nz/Documents/science-and-technical/IR188.pdf|journal=Science and Research Internal Report|volume=188}}</ref><ref name=":6" />

In 2018, a farmer destroyed about one third of Kaitorete spit's ''M. astonii'' plants by spraying and cultivating three paddocks to plant oats.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Harris|first=Dominic|date=1 May 2018|title=Farmer 'destroyed' a third of country's naturally-growing endangered shrubby tororaro plants|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/103507786/court-action-over-alleged-endangered-plant-destruction|access-date=2021-05-25|website=Stuff|language=en-NZ}}</ref>
